title: What the schedule does
objectives: Explain how the noise schedule and the number of steps change the samples.

screens.title: Ten, fifty or two hundred steps
screens.prose: Three noise predictors of the same size were trained on the rings with $T = 10$, 50 and 200 steps. Each schedule ends at the same $\bar\alpha_T$, so only the number of steps differs. The chart shows 300 samples from each; switch between them.
screens.question: Which sample set looks most like two rings?

options.why: Good, but the 200-step rings are thinner: ring shares 0.70 against 0.81.
Its rings are smeared: ring share 0.55.

hints.text: Look at how thin each ring is.
Compare the gap between the rings.

feedback.correct: Right. Ring shares: 0.55, 0.70 and 0.81 for 10, 50 and 200 steps.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare how sharp the rings are.

explain.text: More steps give sharper rings here: ring share 0.55 at 10 steps, 0.70 at 50, 0.81 at 200. Each reverse step is a smaller jump, easier for the net to undo.

screens.title: Signal against noise
screens.prose: The **signal-to-noise ratio** at step $t$ is $\bar\alpha_t/(1 - \bar\alpha_t)$: the variance of the signal part over the variance of the noise. The schedule sets how fast it falls from large to almost 0.
screens.question: What is the ratio at $t = 50$ of our schedule, where $\bar\alpha_{50} \approx 0.0045$? Give a decimal to 4 places.

hints.text: Divide $\bar\alpha_{50}$ by $1 - \bar\alpha_{50}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Signal variance over noise variance.

byKey.inv: You divided the noise by the signal.

explain.text: About 0.0045: the signal is under half a per cent of the noise. Since $\bar\alpha$ is tiny, the ratio is close to $\bar\alpha$ itself.

screens.title: Where three schedules end
screens.prose: The table lists three schedules. The first keeps $\beta_t = 0.1$ for 10 steps.
screens.question: What is $\bar\alpha_{10}$ for the first schedule? Give a decimal to 3 places.

feedback.correct: $0.9^{10} \approx 0.349$: a third of the signal's variance is left.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply ten factors of 0.9.

byKey.sum: You used $1 - \sum\beta_t = 0$. The alphas multiply, and the product stays well above 0.

explain.text: $0.9^{10} \approx 0.349$, so that schedule ends far from pure noise, while the other two end near 0.0045. Sampling from a standard normal would then start in the wrong place.

screens.title: How fast the ratio falls
screens.prose: The curves show $\log_{10}$ of the signal-to-noise ratio against the fraction of the way through each schedule, $t/T$, for $T = 10$, 50 and 200. All three end at the same value.

points.label: T = 50 and 200, almost on top of each other

screens.question: What do more steps buy, if the end point is the same?

options.text: Smaller jumps in the ratio between neighbouring steps
A lower ratio at the end, closer to pure noise
options.why: All three end at the same ratio by construction.

options.text: A faster fall at the start
options.why: The shapes are similar; what changes is how many steps share the fall.

options.text: Nothing, since the curves end in the same place
options.why: The path matters: fewer steps means bigger jumps between neighbouring noise levels.

hints.text: How many steps share the same total fall?
Ten steps must each cover a tenth of it.

feedback.correct: Right. The same fall split into more, smaller steps.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare the size of one step on each curve.

explain.text: With 10 steps each reverse step must undo a large change in the noise level, which a small net does poorly. With 200 the changes are tiny, at 20 times the cost of 10.

screens.title: Quality by number of steps
screens.prose: The ring share of 1,000 samples from each trained net. The data score 1.
screens.question: By how much does the ring share rise from 50 steps to 200? Give a decimal to 2 places.

hints.text: Subtract the 50-step bar from the 200-step bar.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Take the difference of the two bars.

byKey.ten: That is the rise from 10 steps to 50.
byKey.ratio: That is the ratio of the two; the question asks for the difference.

explain.text: Going from 50 to 200 steps adds about 0.11 of ring share at four times the cost per sample; going from 10 to 50 added 0.16. In this toy the gains shrink as steps grow.

screens.title: More steps, always better?
screens.prose: A colleague concludes: "More steps is always better, so use 1,000."
screens.question: What is wrong with that?

options.text: Each step costs a net evaluation, and gains shrank as steps grew
Nothing, since quality rises steadily with $T$
options.why: It rose here, but by less each time (0.16, then 0.11), while the cost grows in proportion.

options.text: More steps always make the samples worse
options.why: Not in this toy: 200 beat 50. The point is cost against a shrinking gain.

options.text: More steps would need a much bigger net
options.why: The same net size trained well at 200 steps here; the cost is in sampling.

hints.text: How many net evaluations does one sample take?
Compare the gains from 10 to 50 and from 50 to 200.

feedback.correct: Right. Steps are a cost traded against quality.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Weigh what each extra step costs.

byKey.right: You extrapolated a rising trend. The gains shrink, and the cost does not.

explain.text: Sampling with $T$ steps costs $T$ net evaluations a sample: 1,000 steps cost five times 200. The gain from 50 to 200 here was 0.11; this is the toy's finding, not a law.

screens.title: One jump
screens.prose: With $T = 1$ the net must go from pure noise to data in a single step. Its ring share is 0.006; the chart shows its samples.
screens.question: Why do the samples bunch near the centre?

options.text: One step can only give the average clean point
The net was not trained for long enough
options.why: It trained for 12,000 steps like the others. One step cannot do better than an average.

options.text: Too much fresh noise is added at the end
options.why: With $T = 1$ no fresh noise is added at all: the single step is the last.

options.text: An unlucky seed for the starting noise
options.why: Any seed gives the same picture: a ring share near 0.01.

hints.text: What is the best squared-error guess of $\mathbf{x}_0$ from pure noise?
An average over both rings.

feedback.correct: Right. A single step can only output a blurred average.
feedback.generic: Not quite. What does minimising squared error give when the input says almost nothing?

explain.text: Trained on squared error, a one-step model outputs the mean of the clean points consistent with its input, and pure noise is consistent with almost all of them. Many small steps let the sampler commit to one ring gradually.

screens.title: An end that is too clean
screens.prose: l13's constant schedule, $\beta_t = 0.01$ for 50 steps, ends at $\bar\alpha_{50} \approx 0.605$. Sampling still starts from $\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})$.
screens.question: What is the standard deviation of the signal part of $\mathbf{x}_{50}$, for a unit-variance coordinate of $\mathbf{x}_0$? Give a decimal to 3 places.

hints.text: Signal part: $\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{50}}\,\mathbf{x}_0$.

feedback.correct: $\sqrt{0.605} \approx 0.778$: most of the data's spread survives.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Take the square root of $\bar\alpha_{50}$.

byKey.abar: That is a share of variance; its square root is the sd.

explain.text: At $t = 50$ real noised data still carry a signal of sd 0.778, so their distribution is far from the standard normal the sampler starts from. The reverse chain begins in the wrong place, and the error never fully washes out.

screens.title: What the schedule controls
screens.prose: A schedule fixes the curve $\bar\alpha_t/(1 - \bar\alpha_t)$. Two things matter: that it ends near 0, so sampling can start from $\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})$, and that it falls in steps small enough for the net to undo. Sampling costs $T$ net evaluations per sample.
screens.question: A schedule ends at $\bar\alpha_T = 0.3$. What should you change?

options.text: Raise the betas or add steps until $\bar\alpha_T$ is near 0
Use fewer steps to save some time
options.why: Fewer steps with the same betas would end even further from noise: $\bar\alpha_T$ rises.

options.text: Nothing, since 0.3 is small enough already
options.why: With 0.3 of the signal's variance left, the starting normal is the wrong distribution.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Where must the forward process end?

explain.text: The sampler assumes $\mathbf{x}_T$ is standard normal, which holds only when $\bar\alpha_T$ is near 0.

screens.title: Paying for steps
screens.prose: A desk prices options on a binomial tree (`trees` l9): more time steps give a more accurate price at more computing cost. A diffusion sampler makes the same trade.
screens.question: What plays the part of the tree's time steps?

options.text: The number of reverse steps $T$
The width of the network
options.why: Width sets the cost of one evaluation; the number of evaluations is the number of steps.

options.text: The number of samples drawn
options.why: More samples tighten estimates of the model's statistics; the steps set each sample's quality.

options.text: The size of the training set
options.why: Training data affect the model, not the cost of drawing one sample.

hints.text: What is repeated, step after step, for every sample?
One net evaluation per step.

feedback.correct: Right. Steps trade cost against accuracy in both.
feedback.generic: Not quite. What does one sample cost?

explain.text: Both are discretisations: a price on a grid, a sample in steps. Past some point extra steps buy little, and the right number depends on what the result is used for.

ideas: The schedule sets how the signal-to-noise ratio $\bar\alpha_t/(1 - \bar\alpha_t)$ falls; it must end near 0 so that sampling can start from $\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})$.
With the end fixed, more steps mean smaller jumps: ring shares 0.01, 0.55, 0.70 and 0.81 at 1, 10, 50 and 200 steps in this toy.
Each step costs one net evaluation per sample, so steps trade cost against a gain that shrinks; one step can only give a blurred average.

formula.name: Signal-to-noise ratio
formula.note: It should fall to near 0 by $t = T$.

summary.trap: Assuming more steps is always better: cost grows in proportion while the gain shrinks.

quiz.question: What is the signal-to-noise ratio? Give a decimal.

explain.text: $0.2/0.8 = 0.25$: the signal's variance is a quarter of the noise's.

quiz.prose: Sampler A uses 50 steps and sampler B 200, with the same net.
quiz.question: How many times as many net evaluations does B need per sample?

feedback.generic: Not quite. One evaluation per step.

byKey.same: The net is the same, but it runs once per step.

explain.text: Each step evaluates the net once, so 200 steps cost 4 times 50.

quiz.prose: A diffusion model is trained with a single step, $T = 1$.
quiz.question: What do its samples look like?

options.text: A blurred average near the centre
Perfect copies of the data
options.why: One step from pure noise cannot commit to one part of the data.

options.text: Pure noise
options.why: The step does remove noise; it lands on an average.

feedback.generic: Not quite. What is the best one-step guess from noise?

explain.text: From pure noise the squared-error-optimal guess is close to the data's mean, so one-step samples blur together.
